questions.explanation: Ecclesiastes 9:13-18 holds two truths in tension: first, quiet wisdom is genuinely superior to military hardware ('better than weapons of war'); second, a status-obsessed world will happily accept rescue from a poor wise man during an emergency and immediately ignore him the next morning.

questions.question: After spending ten chapters proving that human beings cannot predict the future or eliminate risk, how does the Teacher apply that uncertainty to daily work, generosity, and decision-making in Ecclesiastes 11:1–6 ('He who observes the wind will not sow, and he who regards the clouds will not reap')?
options: Instead of letting uncertainty paralyze you into waiting for guaranteed, risk-free conditions that never arrive, cast your bread generously, diversify your efforts ('give a portion to seven, or even to eight'), and sow your seed morning and evening—precisely because you do not know which effort will succeed.
Because the future is unpredictable, you should stop planting crops altogether and wait passively for rain.
You should hire royal astrologers to predict the exact weather before investing a single shekel.
You should hoard all your grain in a single locked barn and never share with anyone until you are old.
questions.explanation: Ecclesiastes 11:1-6 turns human ignorance of the future from an excuse for analysis paralysis ('watching the wind and clouds') into a call for bold, diversified action and open-handed generosity.

questions.question: In Song of Solomon 2:15, what does the couple say must be caught to protect their blossoming vineyard?
options: Wild birds flying in the sky
The little foxes that ruin vineyards
Heavy rain clouds from the north
Strangers walking along the road
questions.explanation: Song of Solomon 2:15 uses 'the little foxes that spoil the vineyards' while the vines are in blossom to picture catching small, neglected problems before they ruin a relationship.

questions.question: In Song of Solomon 6:3, how does the bride describe her bond with her beloved?
options: He is my royal tax collector
We are strangers from distant lands
I am my beloved's and he is mine
Our families signed a business deal
questions.explanation: Song of Solomon 6:3 ('I am my beloved's and my beloved is mine') expresses mutual belonging, trust, and exclusive devotion rather than one-sided ownership.

questions.question: According to Song of Solomon 8:7, what happens if someone tries to buy real love with money?
options: They win the best marriage in town
They must pay extra temple tax
They receive love for one year
Their offer is completely despised
questions.explanation: Song of Solomon 8:7 states that many waters cannot quench love, and if someone offered all the wealth of their house to buy love, it would be utterly scorned.

questions.question: Three times in Song of Solomon (2:7, 3:5, 8:4), the bride charges the daughters of Jerusalem 'not to stir up or awaken love until it pleases.' What wisdom does this refrain teach?
options: Powerful romantic desire requires patient timing rather than premature forcing.
Marriages should only be arranged by royal tax collectors in Jerusalem.
Romantic love is dangerous and should be suppressed for economic alliances.
Couples must refuse all contact with extended family and neighbors.
questions.explanation: In a book that celebrates passionate romance, the repeated refrain in 2:7, 3:5, and 8:4 warns against artificially rushing or awakening desire before its rightful season and covenant commitment.

questions.question: In Song of Solomon 5:2–8, when the beloved knocks at night, the bride hesitates with flimsy excuses about having washed her feet—and finds him gone when she finally opens the door. What relational dynamic does this scene capture?
options: That locking doors at night was illegal inside the city of Jerusalem.
How taking a partner for granted through lazy complacency creates painful distance.
That the groom was actually a foreign spy testing the city guards.
That couples should live in separate towns so they never argue.
questions.explanation: Song of Solomon 5:2-6 realistically portrays relational friction inside love: meeting a partner's vulnerable initiative with self-absorbed convenience ('how can I put on my garment?') leads to a painful season of searching and repair.

questions.question: In Song of Solomon 8:11–12, why does the speaker contrast King Solomon's massive vineyard leased to tenants for a thousand silver pieces with 'my own vineyard, which is before me'?
options: To show that large royal farms are more profitable than family plots.
To announce plans to sell their private vineyard to pay family debts.
To declare that personal, exclusive devotion beats Solomon's outsourced harem wealth.
To accuse northern tenant farmers of cheating the crown out of silver.
questions.explanation: In Song of Solomon 8:11-12, the speaker tells Solomon he can keep his thousand pieces of silver and leased-out empire, because tending one's own singular relationship firsthand cannot be outsourced.

questions.question: In the opening chapter of Song of Solomon (1:5–6), the bride explains to the aristocratic court women of Jerusalem that she is sun-darkened because her brothers were angry with her and forced her to work outdoors keeping their vineyards, adding wistfully, 'my own vineyard I have not kept!' How does this opening vulnerability connect to her closing declaration in 8:12 ('My vineyard, my very own, is before me')?
options: She sues her brothers in the royal court in chapter 8 and wins back the legal title to their agricultural estate.
She abandons farming completely and moves into the winter palace in Susa so she never has to see a vineyard again.
She hires foreign servants in chapter 8 to work her brothers' land while she collects two hundred pieces of silver.

The book traces a full-circle arc of personal agency and healing: she begins in chapter 1 overextended, insecure under the gaze of elite insiders, and forced to tend everyone else's demands at the expense of her own life ('my own vineyard I have not kept'), and finishes in chapter 8 secure in covenant love and fully in charge of her own 'vineyard.'
questions.explanation: Comparing Song of Solomon 1:6 with 8:12 reveals a cohesive psychological arc across the poem: moving from an exploited young woman self-conscious about her sunburned laborer's skin and depleted by her brothers' demands ('my own vineyard I have not kept') to confident self-possession and mutual love ('my own vineyard is before me').

questions.question: In Song of Solomon 5:9, after the bride frantically searches the city streets for her departed beloved following her own indifference at the door, the daughters of Jerusalem ask her a skeptical question: 'What is your beloved more than another beloved, that you thus adjure us?' How does that question trigger the turning point of their reconciliation in chapters 5–6?
options: Forced to articulate aloud why he is irreplaceable to her (verses 10–16), rehearsing his character and beauty from head to toe reawakens her own appreciation, ends her self-absorption, and leads her concluded affirmation: 'This is my beloved and this is my friend.'
She realizes she cannot think of any reason he is special and decides to return to her brothers' house in the country.
She gets angry at the daughters of Jerusalem and orders the city watchmen to arrest them for interfering.
She offers the daughters of Jerusalem a reward of gold rings if they can describe what her beloved looks like.
questions.explanation: Song of Solomon 5:9-16 shows how gratitude repairs relational drift: when challenged by outsiders to explain what makes her beloved any different from anyone else, verbally recounting his worth ('he is altogether desirable—this is my beloved and this is my friend') dissolves the distance between them.

questions.question: Why is the Song of Solomon placed within the Old Testament Wisdom Literature alongside Proverbs and Ecclesiastes, and why does its theological climax in 8:6–7 describe covenant love not as a gentle, sentimental feeling, but as 'strong as death, jealousy (ardent devotion) as fierce as the grave; its flashes are flashes of fire, the very flame of the Lord'?
options: Because the book warns that romantic love always leads to premature death and should be avoided by wise scholars.

Because true biblical wisdom rejects both cynical asceticism (treating the physical body as evil) and casual consumerism (treating intimacy as a disposable recreation)—teaching that authentic covenant love is a sacred fire sourced in God Himself that demands exclusive, unyielding commitment as serious and irreversible as death.
Because King Solomon wrote the poem to justify collecting seven hundred foreign wives for diplomatic treaties.
Because ancient wedding contracts required the bride and groom to walk through a literal fire outside the city gate.
questions.explanation: Song of Solomon 8:6-7 is the theological apex of the book: where cultures either idolize sex as a casual transaction or despise it as unspiritual, Wisdom Literature celebrates covenant love as 'the very flame of the Lord'—too fierce to be played with casually and too sacred to be bought with money.

questions.question: In Psalm 27, why is David unafraid even if an army surrounds him?
options: Because the Lord is his light and stronghold
Because his city walls are too high to climb
Because he hired foreign mercenaries for gold
Because his enemies ran out of food and water
questions.explanation: David anchors his courage not in military superiority, but in the conviction that when God is your light and stronghold, human intimidation loses its grip.

questions.question: When the traveler in Psalm 121 looks up at the hills, where does help come from?
options: From the royal guards stationed on the ridge
From the Lord, who made heaven and earth
From the merchant caravan traveling behind him
From the watchtowers built along the road
questions.explanation: Psalm 121 shifts the traveler's eyes past the intimidating terrain to the Creator who never slumbers or sleeps while watching over the journey.

questions.question: In Psalm 32, what physical and emotional toll does David describe during the period when he kept silent and refused to admit his wrongdoing?
options: He slept peacefully because no one in the palace knew his secret
He forgot all about his mistake by throwing himself into military campaigns
His strength dried up like summer heat and his bones felt worn out all day long
He blamed his advisors publicly so his conscience would feel lighter
questions.explanation: Psalm 32:3-5 is a remarkably modern description of psychosomatic guilt: hiding a wrong drains the body's vitality like a fever, while honest confession immediately releases the pressure.

questions.question: In Psalm 90 (the prayer of Moses), what practical habit does he ask God to teach us in light of how brief and fragile human life is?
options: To build monuments of stone so future generations remember our names
To avoid taking any risks that might shorten our comfortable years
To withdraw from society and spend our days in silent isolation
To number our days intentionally so that we gain a heart of wisdom
questions.explanation: Denying mortality breeds wasted time and trivial priorities; Moses argues that squarely facing the finite count of our days is what disciplines the mind into wisdom.

questions.question: Why does Psalm 103 use the specific geometry of 'as far as the east is from the west' rather than north from south to describe how far God removes transgressions, and what view of human nature grounds that mercy?
options: East and west never meet, and God remembers our frame that we are fragile dust rather than invincible beings
East and west marked the borders of the Israelite kingdom, proving mercy only applies inside the land
The sunrise and sunset happen every twenty-four hours, meaning sins must be re-atoned for every single evening
Ancient navigators only measured latitude, so east and west represented a short, measurable distance
questions.explanation: Unlike north and south (which meet at the poles), east and west are infinite opposing directions, and Psalm 103:14 grounds this boundless patience in God's realism that humans are made of dust.

questions.question: In Psalm 130, the writer notes that if God kept a permanent ledger of every human failure, no one could stand. What counter-intuitive conclusion does he draw in the very next verse about why people revere God?
options: People revere God because they are terrified that one more mistake will trigger instant destruction
With God there is forgiveness, and it is that very mercy rather than terror of a ledger that produces genuine reverence
People revere God only when they believe their good deeds outweigh their past mistakes
God erases the moral law entirely so that human actions no longer carry any spiritual weight
questions.explanation: Human tyrants assume mercy breeds disrespect and only relentless score-keeping keeps people in line; Psalm 130:4 flips that psychology upside down: 'But with you there is forgiveness, so that you may be revered.'
